content.title: About
content.content: Corn chips, flavored (Fritos) are crunchy corn snacks coated with a savory seasoning. Made from whole‑grain corn, they are fried to a golden crisp and dusted with spices that give a classic salty‑cheese flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Fritos were first introduced in the United States in 1932 by The Frito Company.
The original flavor is cheese, but there are also chili, barbecue, and other variants.
Corn chips are naturally gluten‑free, making them suitable for gluten‑free diets.
The early Fritos packaging featured a bright red design with corn kernels.
In 1961 The Frito Company merged with PepsiCo, forming Frito‑Lay.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Corn provides slowly digestible carbs that supply steady energy and help keep you feeling full.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestive health and can aid in blood‑sugar regulation.

items.title: Low in trans fats
items.content: Modern Fritos recipes use non‑hydrogenated oils, reducing trans‑fat content.

items.title: Enriched with B‑vitamins
items.content: During processing, thiamine and niacin are often added to support metabolism.

items.title: Gluten‑free
items.content: Suitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Excess salt can raise blood pressure when consumed frequently.

items.title: Calorie dense
items.content: Portion control is important, especially for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Corn allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may experience allergic reactions to corn products.

items.title: Fat content
items.content: While trans fats are low, the snack does contain vegetable oils that may be high in saturated fats.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Corn chips, flavored (Fritos) are perfect as a standalone snack, tossed into salads, used as a base for toppings (e.g., in tacos), or served with dips such as salsa, guacamole, or cheese sauce.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the chips in the original bag or an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For longer shelf life, store them in the refrigerator to maintain crispness and prevent oil oxidation.

content.title: About
content.content: Frog legs are the edible muscles of a frog's hind limbs, traditionally used in French, Chinese, and Southeast Asian cuisines. They have a delicate, slightly sweet flavor reminiscent of chicken and a firm yet tender texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Frog legs are considered a delicacy in France, where they are often served as "cuisses de grenouille".
In China, frog legs are commonly cooked in a soy‑ginger‑garlic sauce.
They contain more protein per gram than chicken breast while being low in fat.
Frogs are harvested during the breeding season when the muscles are at their densest.
Traditionally the legs are dusted in flour or starch before frying to create a crisp crust.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Frog legs provide about 16 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: They contain less than 2 g of fat per 100 g, most of it polyunsaturated.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Frog legs supply vitamin B12, niacin, and riboflavin, which are important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: They are a good source of iron, zinc, and phosphorus, contributing to blood health and bone strength.

items.title: Low calorie density
items.content: Approximately 70 kcal per 100 g, making them suitable for calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: Allergy cross‑reactivity
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions, especially those sensitive to seafood or reptiles.

items.title: Parasitic contamination
items.content: Improperly processed legs can harbor parasites; cook thoroughly to at least 70 °C.

items.title: Purine content
items.content: High purine levels may exacerbate gout in susceptible people.

items.title: Environmental restrictions
items.content: Harvesting of wild frogs is regulated in many areas; purchase only from certified suppliers.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Frog legs can be sautéed, braised, steamed, or baked. They are often marinated in wine, garlic, and herbs, then lightly coated in flour and quickly fried until golden. Serve with lemon, butter‑herb sauce, or a light vinaigrette.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh legs refrigerated at 0–2 °C in an airtight container for up to 2 days. Frozen legs retain quality for up to 3 months at –18 °C. Rinse under cold water and pat dry before cooking.

stuffed-shells-with-chicken-with-tomato-.title: Stuffed shells with chicken and tomato sauce

content.title: About
content.content: Stuffed shells are large pasta shells filled with a mixture of chicken breast, cheese, and herbs, baked in a flavorful tomato sauce. The dish is a staple of Italian-inspired cuisine and is often served as a hearty lunch or dinner.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Traditionally shells are filled with ricotta and spinach, but the chicken version has become popular in the United States.
The tomato sauce is usually made from ripe tomatoes, basil, and olive oil.
Chicken makes the filling lighter than a beef-based version.
The dish can be prepared ahead of time and reheated, making it a family favorite.
Some regions top the shells with grated Parmesan and fresh herbs before serving.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Chicken provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Both chicken and tomato sauce contain B6 and B12, supporting nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Lycopene in tomatoes
items.content: Tomatoes are high in lycopene, an antioxidant linked to reduced risk of certain chronic diseases.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Compared with beef‑based fillings, chicken contains less saturated fat.

items.title: Calcium from cheese
items.content: Cheese adds calcium, important for bone and teeth health.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Cheese in the filling can trigger reactions in people with lactose intolerance or milk allergy.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Tomato sauce often contains added salt; choose a low‑sodium version if you watch your sodium intake.

items.title: Food poisoning
items.content: Chicken must be cooked thoroughly to eliminate the risk of salmonella.

items.title: Gluten in pasta
items.content: Traditional shells are made from wheat and contain gluten; gluten‑free shells are needed for those with celiac disease.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve hot, sprinkled with grated Parmesan and fresh basil. Pair with a green salad or steamed vegetables. Leftovers reheat well in the oven or microwave.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the cooked dish in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. It can be frozen for up to 2 months; reheat to an internal temperature of 75 °C before serving.
